papers.title: Towards an active inference account of deep meditative deconstruction.
papers.abstract: This paper explores the intersection of the deep meditative deconstruction resulting from Buddhist meditative practice, specifically through the defabrication process, with the active inference framework (AIF). We propose that defabrication, central to Buddhist meditation, can be understood as a computational process whereby the repeated release of mental tension-associated with clinging and aversion-drives inference progressively lower in an agent's hierarchical generative model. By casting the release of mental tension as a reduction in hierarchical level-specific precision over beliefs about hidden causes, we demonstrate how the phenomenology of defabrication naturally arises from the resultant system dynamics. This approach enables a computational interpretation of Buddhist meditative states, such as the jhānas, and core concepts like equanimity and stillness. More broadly, it advances a computational phenomenology of meditative deconstruction. Finally, we illustrate the deconstruction process under AIF by extending it to the cessation of phenomenal experience, suggesting this offers insight into core-knowledge structuring and the generation of experience.

papers.title: A curriculum-based program introducing mindfulness and reflection to GP trainees.
papers.abstract: AIM: To explore participant's experience of a pilot, curriculum-based mindfulness and personal reflection program on the resilience levels and well-being of 3rd year trainee General Practitioners (GP's). METHODS: 3rd year trainee GP's were invited to participate in four morning sessions, plus one retreat day program which was incorporated into the trainees 3rd year curriculum. Volunteers from the intervention group were then invited to take part in a focus group aimed at exploring their experiences and perspectives in greater depth. The qualitative data gathered from the focus group was analysed using thematic analysis to identify common themes and insights. RESULTS: The focus group identified a number of themes including; quality of programme delivery and content, the experience of a safe space, the relevance of the content to the wider GP role, the uptake of skills such as mindfulness and the impact of these skills on stress management. Limitations and challenges to sustainable practice were also identified. DISCUSSION: Medical students are at high risk of psychological distress, depression, and suicidality. The health and well-being of doctors is key to supporting the quality and safety of patient care. More needs to be done to build a sustainable and resilience work force for the future.

papers.title: Group and online application of the Unified Protocol in Argentina: controlled pilot study.
papers.abstract: Emotional disorders (ED), including anxiety and depression, are highly prevalent in Argentina and share dysfunctional emotional regulation mechanisms. The Unified Protocol (UP) is a transdiagnostic intervention designed to address these common processes. This is the first randomized controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate its effectiveness on a group and online format in the Argentinian population. papers.title: The Association Between Physical Exercise and Sleep Quality Among Junior Middle School Students: The Mediating Role of Social Support and the Moderating Role of Mindfulness.
papers.abstract: This study explores the relationship between physical exercise and sleep quality, focusing on the mediating role of social support and the moderating role of mindfulness. The sample included 1,023 junior middle school students (51.22% females; mean age = 13.59 ± 0.84 years). Participants completed measures of physical exercise, sleep quality, social support, and mindfulness. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, bias-corrected bootstrap procedures, and Hayes' PROCESS macro for SPSS (Models 4 and 59). The results showed that 24.73% of the participants screened positive for sleep problems (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) > 7), and physical exercise was significantly positively associated with sleep quality. Social support played a significant mediating role in the relationship between physical exercise and sleep quality. Mindfulness significantly moderated the association between social support and sleep quality and the residual direct association between physical exercise and sleep quality, but did not significantly moderate the association between physical exercise and social support. At higher levels of mindfulness, the positive associations of physical exercise and social support with sleep quality were stronger. These findings revealed the roles of social support and mindfulness in the association between physical exercise and sleep quality and provided a new perspective for sleep-health promotion among junior middle school students. Schools, families, and communities should coordinate efforts to promote physical exercise, strengthen social support, and cultivate mindfulness among junior middle school students.

papers.title: Mindfulness- and relaxation-based interventions for Premenstrual Syndrome: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) affects many women of reproductive age, often disrupting daily activities. Mindfulness- and relaxation-based techniques, such as yoga and progressive muscle relaxation techniques, can alleviate both physical and psychosocial symptoms associated with PMS. This systematic review synthesized existing evidence on the effects of mindfulness and relaxation interventions on the physical and psychosocial functioning of women experiencing PMS. The searches were conducted across five databases (PubMed, CINAHL Complete, ProQuest, MasterFILE Complete, and JSTOR Life Sciences) and two publisher websites (Wiley and Mary Ann Liebert, Inc.). This review followed the PRISMA guidelines and evaluated the quality of individual studies. Included were reproductive-age women using mindfulness or relaxation techniques for premenstrual symptoms in peer-reviewed intervention studies published between December 2015 and December 2025. This review included 22 studies involving 1,598 participants, comprising 13 RCTs, 7 non-RCTs, and 2 studies without a control group. The interventions included yoga (4), guided imagery (2), mindfulness-based cognitive behavioral therapy (2), progressive muscle relaxation (6), and other programs (5). One study each used an occupational therapy intervention, meditation, and counseling. The interventions typically lasted 20-60 minutes (18/22), and 19 studies evaluated PMS symptom severity. Mindfulness-and relaxation-based interventions decreased physical symptoms such as pain and fatigue, and psychosocial symptoms such as anxiety, depression, stress, and sexual function, resulting in an improved quality of life. Mindfulness- and relaxation-based interventions are associated with meaningful improvements in psychosocial, physical, and functional outcomes for PMS, although the evidence remains limited. These approaches may be considered as components of comprehensive, occupation-based care to support participation and overall well-being.
